strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with compelling argument that RGB generation introduces unnecessary overhead for motion prediction
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101) with multiple metrics (FVMD, LRTL, Best-of-K) and user study validation
Extensive reproducibility details including hyperparameters, model configurations, training resources, and evaluation protocols enabling reproduction
Strong empirical results on synthetic data with consistent improvements over regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE) and competitive results vs. fine-tuned video generators
Novel insight demonstrated convincingly in Section 4.3: direct trajectory generation is more effective than extracting motion from RGB videos through careful modality ablation
Introduces useful LRTL metric for evaluating physical plausibility (rigidity preservation) of predicted trajectories
Significant computational efficiency gains (220M vs 14000M parameters, 2.9s vs 248s inference) with practical implications for deployment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (flow matching, VAE, Latte architecture) to a different output modality rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithms

Weak real-world validation despite claims about practical applications: Physics101 results are marginal (28.62 vs 30.08 MSE vs WAN), only qualitative results on real-world generalization from Physion, acknowledged computational resource constraints prevented large-scale real-world evaluation

Experimental fairness concerns: regression baseline comparison uses k=8 samples for proposed method vs k=1 for baselines then reports 'Min' metric which is oracle-like; video generators trained on billions of videos then fine-tuned on synthetic data; Track2Act significantly modified (8→24 frames, 400→1024 points)

Multimodality learning unclear: model trained with only one ground truth per condition but must learn multimodal distribution; VAE ablation shows mixed results (better on LIBERO, worse on Physics101), suggesting dataset-dependent effectiveness; limited evidence for avoiding mode collapse beyond Figure 7

Evaluation metric limitations: FVMD depends entirely on CoTracker biases, LRTL assumes rigidity (not applicable to fluids/deformable objects), Best-of-K is artificial (single sample needed in practice), Table 21 shows metric sensitivity to number of samples

Limited scope: quasi-dense grids may not handle sparse moving objects well, strong performance only on Kubric (simple primitives), no comparison with segmentation-aware or object-centric methods, performance degrades on out-of-distribution Kubric variants

Incomplete analysis: mechanism for why RGB produces non-rigid motion beyond 'overhead' not deeply explored, no failure case analysis, unclear what physical priors model learns, limited justification for patch size/downsampling factor choices, β parameter mostly fixed

Mixed generalization evidence across datasets: Kubric strong, LIBERO moderate, Physics101 comparable/marginal to WAN, real-world only qualitative on small datasets, unclear when practitioners should prefer this over video generation
Strong claims about video generators 'struggling' based primarily on synthetic scenarios (Kubric); Figure 1 comparison somewhat unfair given WAN's different optimization objectives on diverse data
No quantitative evidence that single ground truth training successfully produces meaningful multimodal distributions; ablation suggests this may be a fundamental limitation depending on dataset

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight that trajectory generation is simpler than pixel generation for motion prediction
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, Physion) with complementary metrics (FVMD, LRTL, Best-of-K, user study)
Decisive modality ablation (Table 6) fixing architecture and varying only output modality provides strong evidence for the hypothesis
Extensive reproducibility details including hyperparameters, training times, and computational requirements
Consistent empirical improvements over regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE) and Track2Act on controlled benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VAE for trajectory encoding, flow matching, and spatio-temporal transformers are all standard techniques adapted from prior work without algorithmic innovation

Unfair comparison with video generators: they were trained for general purpose diverse video generation not specialized physics prediction; comparison conflates different training objectives and fine-tuning constraints handicap baselines
Real-world generalization not convincingly demonstrated: Physics101 shows only marginal improvements with overlapping error ranges; Physion-to-real transfer (A.3) is qualitative only

Weak evaluation metrics for generative models: Best-of-K encourages generating many samples rather than good average quality; FVMD uses histograms missing fine-grained structure; LRTL rigidity metric insufficient for non-rigid objects; no statistical significance testing

VAE design questionable: β=1e-6 essentially disables KL regularization making it an autoencoder; inconsistent contribution where VAE hurts Physics101 performance (Table 14); no ablation of flow matching directly on coordinates
User study provides only marginal confirmation: 52% preference over 25% random, 20 users, 16 scenes, ELO scores show overlap with baselines
Overstated claims about video generators: criticizes them for lacking learned behaviors (object permanence) that should emerge from data; conflates different training paradigms without justification

Comparison fairness issues: method designed specifically for physics simulation data; video generators adapted from general pretraining; post-hoc CoTracker introduces tracking error absent in trajectory method
Limited to structured/synthetic domains with poor real-world applicability; all quantitative real-world evaluation (Physics101) shows results comparable to baselines
Missing technical ablations: DINOv2 cross-attention contribution not isolated; no direct flow matching on raw coordinates comparison; VAE necessity unexplored

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight that trajectory generation is fundamentally better suited for motion prediction than RGB video generation, demonstrated convincingly through modality ablation (Section 4.3, Table 6)

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, Physion) with diverse metrics (Best-of-K, FVMD, LRTL) and extensive comparisons against regression, trajectory, and video generation baselines
Strong and consistent empirical results: outperforms all baseline categories, even state-of-the-art video generators fine-tuned on task data, with 52% user preference vs 20-28% for baselines
Excellent reproducibility: extensive implementation details, complete hyperparameters, training resources, architectural diagrams, and ~32 GPU-day compute specification enabling easy reproduction

Rigorous ablation studies validating design choices (VAE necessity for multimodality, model scale, trajectory source) and compelling analysis of why trajectory approach succeeds (object permanence, temporal coherence, low-rank structure)
Practical efficiency advantages: 100× faster inference (2.9s vs 248s), 65× smaller model (220M vs 14B parameters) than WAN while achieving superior motion accuracy

Technically sound methodology: appropriate application of VAE + flow matching for stochastic trajectory modeling with careful experimental protocol, proper train/val/test splits, and principled model selection criteria
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: primarily adapts Latte (Ma et al., 2025) with application-specific modifications (image conditioning, trajectory tokenization) rather than introducing novel architectural components; main contribution is problem formulation and modality choice rather than technical innovation

Critical unresolved limitation: single ground truth trajectory per training sample (Section 3.3) requires model to infer multimodality from 'nearby training examples,' but this assumption is never empirically validated; unclear whether denoiser learns proper multimodal distribution or collapses to mode despite VAE demonstrating interpolation capability

Significantly limited real-world evaluation: Physics101 uses only 1 sample per initial condition prohibiting distributional metrics; Physion-to-real generalization (Section A.3) is purely qualitative with very small test set; no large-scale real-world dataset experiments; substantially weakens practical applicability claims

Scope narrowly constrained to structured synthetic scenes: geometric primitives in Kubric don't capture real-world complexity; Physics101 limited to specific scenarios (fall, liquid, ramp, spring); no evaluation on human motion, articulated objects, or camera motion; short prediction horizons (16-30 frames/0.7-1.25s); quasi-dense grids still quite sparse

Questionable baseline fairness: video generators (WAN, SVD) are general-purpose models pre-trained on billions of videos, not designed for physics prediction; while fine-tuning helps, comparison pits task-specific trained-from-scratch model against off-the-shelf systems adapted post-hoc; should be more explicitly acknowledged

Metric design concerns: Best-of-K can bias toward higher diversity but lower accuracy; FVMD (histogram-based) may miss certain motion errors; LRTL specific to rigid objects; no unified metric comprehensively captures motion quality; user study relatively small (20 subjects, 16 scenes)

Training data scalability unclear: relies on pseudo-labeled trajectories from CoTracker (which has ~91% accuracy, Table 20); practical implications of error propagation for real-world scaling not thoroughly explored; fundamental tension between single-trajectory training and multimodal test-time sampling needs deeper investigation

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with practical applications in robotics and control
Strong core insight that direct trajectory generation is more efficient than RGB generation; modality ablation (Table 6) provides convincing evidence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5+ datasets with diverse baselines (regression, diffusion, large-scale video generators) and multiple metrics
Consistent empirical improvements over strong baselines including state-of-the-art video generators; user study provides external validation
Extensive reproducibility documentation including hyperparameters, ablations, implementation details, and estimated computational requirements
Rigorous comparison methodology that minimizes architectural differences when isolating the trajectory vs. RGB modality choice
Demonstrates that large-scale pretraining doesn't guarantee motion prediction accuracy, challenging common assumptions
weaknesses: Critical real-world evaluation gap: Physics101 and Cityscapes use CoTracker pseudo-labels rather than ground truth; real-world generalization is only qualitative (Fig. 7), undermining applicability claims to robotics/autonomous systems

Inconsistent results on core design choices: VAE ablation (Table 16) shows worse performance on Physics101 (31.67 vs 28.62); latent space smoothness justification (Section 3.3) lacks empirical validation

Comparison with video generators may not be entirely fair: massive pretraining on billions of videos is fundamentally different from domain-specific training; 'same training time' does not equate to comparable computational budgets
Limited architectural novelty: heavy adaptation of existing Latte blocks with modifications (gated cross-attention, QK norm); main contribution is conceptual rather than technical

Evaluation methodology concerns: single pseudo ground truth per condition on real data prevents distributional assessment; Best-of-K metric design favors sample diversity; LRTL rigidity metric assumes low-rank structure may not generalize

Incomplete generalization analysis: OOD performance degrades (Table 4); behavior at different image resolutions and with edge-case object types not explored; direct dependency on CoTracker quality not discussed

Training-inference mismatch underdeveloped: single ground truth during training but multiple at inference; latent smoothness solution lacks rigorous justification beyond interpolation visualization (Fig. 15)

strengths: Clear problem motivation and well-reasoned formulation of motion forecasting as trajectory generation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets with appropriate metrics (distributional, point-wise, and physical plausibility)
Compelling modality ablation (Table 6) demonstrating that trajectories are better than pixels for motion generation
Consistent improvements over multiple baselines including fine-tuned large video models
Extensive reproducibility details with hyperparameters, architecture specifications, and hardware requirements
Thoughtful ablation studies on design choices (grid density, VAE, model scale)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily applies existing VAE+flow matching techniques to trajectory domain with minor architectural modifications
Insufficient real-world validation: Physics101 has single pseudo ground-truth per condition; Cityscapes is small-scale; Physion→real generalization is qualitative only

Unfair baseline comparisons: (1) method predicts 1024-point grids vs. baselines optimized for 32 points; (2) fine-tuning large video models on simple synthetic Kubric may disadvantage them; (3) Track2Act substantially modified (points, horizon, training setup)
Mixed results on VAE necessity—ablations show VAE hurts performance on Physics101 (Table 16); no exploration of alternative latent representations
Evaluation concerns: FVMD metric acknowledged as coarse; LRTL metric (rank-5) lacks sensitivity analysis; single ground-truth per condition limits robustness assessment
Missing failure analysis—no discussion of where method fails, what motion types are hard, or sensitivity to different object types and interactions
Statistical rigor lacking: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; user study small (16 scenes, 20 users)

Paper length and organization—excessive appendix content; some overstatements (e.g., 'state-of-the-art generators struggle' may reflect suboptimal tuning for synthetic physics rather than fundamental limitations)

strengths: Clear problem motivation with strong empirical evidence that video generators fail at motion prediction despite massive pretraining
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, Cityscapes, Physion) with fair baseline comparisons and proper fine-tuning
Powerful modality ablation (Section 4.3) that isolates the contribution by holding architecture constant and varying only output modality
Rigorous evaluation with complementary metrics (FVMD, LRTL, Best-of-K MSE) that go beyond standard video generation metrics to assess physical plausibility
Practical efficiency: 50-60× fewer parameters and 50-500× faster inference than video baselines, enabling edge deployment
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architectural specifications, training resources, and extensive ablations in appendix
Strong empirical results validated by user study (52% preference over fine-tuned WAN and SVD)
Thorough supplementary material including design choice ablations, multi-frame extension, and qualitative analysis
weaknesses: Limited real-world evaluation: Physics101 uses only 1 sample per scene (no distributional assessment), Cityscapes is modest in scale, and Physion→real generalization is only qualitative with a small custom dataset

Training from single ground-truth futures per scene is problematic for learning multi-modal distributions; limited analysis of whether sampled trajectories match true distribution or represent interpolation between nearby training examples

Architectural novelty is limited: core architecture directly borrowed from Latte with straightforward modifications; main contribution is output modality rather than novel methods or architectural innovations

Some evaluation metrics favor the proposed method: Best-of-K is artificial (assumes oracle selection), metric sensitivity to sample count (Table 24), and 'Min' aggregation cherry-picks best samples unrealistically
Incomplete characterization of when trajectory prediction should be preferred over video generation; unclear applicability boundaries and downstream task compatibility
VAE ablation results mixed on real data (Table 16): VAE sometimes hurts Physics101 performance; authors emphasize synthetic results but real-world evidence is inconclusive
Limited temporal horizon exploration: all experiments use short predictions (16-30 frames); unclear how error accumulates at longer horizons
Sparse failure mode analysis: occlusions mentioned but not systematically evaluated; complex interactions and deformable bodies under-explored
'Quasi-dense' grids remain quite sparse (1024 points for 256×256 image = 1 point per 64 pixels); grid density choices appear somewhat arbitrary

Comparison fairness concerns: video generators designed for general image-to-video task, not physics prediction; comparing billion-parameter general models to specialized models may not be entirely fair
